name: African feminism
summary: African feminism is a set of theories and movements, not one doctrine, that seek equality and improved status for women on the continent while grounding the project in African cultures and histories rather than Western models. Its mainstream holds that patriarchy was strengthened by colonialism and persists through neo-colonial structures, that oppressions of sex, class and race combine, and that men should be partners in change. Strands such as nego-feminism, stiwanism and Motherism differ on method (negotiation versus transformation), on family and motherhood, and especially on sexuality.
scope: The mainstream of continental African feminisms since the 1980s as set out by Molara Ogundipe-Leslie (stiwanism), Obioma Nnaemeka (nego-feminism) and the 2003 Maputo Protocol, with Motherism and Awa Thiam's multiple jeopardy as supporting strands. Diaspora-focused womanism and Africana womanism and particular national women's movements are excluded. Much of the test (economics, defence, tech) is outside what the sources address, so many answers are low-confidence inferences.

sources.usedFor: Stiwanism: structural and colonial account of patriarchy, work with men, rejection of Euro-American definitions.

public-ownership.rationale: African feminist writing is concerned with class and neo-colonial structures but does not set out a position on nationalising industries.

worker-ownership.rationale: The sources discuss women's cooperative and savings practices but give no view on worker ownership of firms.

surveillance-ok.rationale: African feminist writing has no recorded stance on surveillance and terrorism.

decide-locally.rationale: Nnaemeka values locally defined priorities in development, yet feminists also use national and continental law for women's rights, so this is split.

traditional-family.rationale: Sources show many African feminists value family and communalism (Motherism, Aidoo) while fighting patriarchal norms within it, so they are split on this wording.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Nyanzi notes the bulk of African feminists resist challenging heterosexism while a minority of queer feminists push for it, so adherents are split.

abortion-legal.rationale: Article 14 of the Maputo Protocol permits abortion only in limited cases such as rape, incest and risk to health, which falls short of legal in most cases.

more-religion-public.rationale: Islamic and Christian-influenced feminisms exist alongside secular ones, and the sources show no consensus on religion's public role.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: African feminists tie women's status to colonial and racial hierarchies and reject Western white-feminist framing, which supports active correction of historical injustice.

gender-social-construct.rationale: The sources describe African feminisms as aiming to change culture as it affects women, treating gender roles as made by societies and colonialism, though some stress complementarity.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: African feminists defend African cultural practice against Western imposition (Nnaemeka) but also aim to modify culture where it harms women (Nkealah).

gradual-change.rationale: Nego-feminism and snail-sense feminism favour negotiated, strategic progress while stiwanism calls for comprehensive transformation, so the school is split.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Feminists use AU and UN instruments such as the Maputo Protocol, yet distrust Western-led international agendas (Nnaemeka), so views are mixed.

nation-first.rationale: No documented position; anti-imperial leanings are balanced by use of international women's rights law.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Nnaemeka criticises Western feminists who claim a moral duty to rescue African women, implying scepticism of interventions in their name.

experts-over-public.rationale: Nnaemeka argues African women's knowledge is marginalised by outside experts and theory makers, implying distrust of expert rule.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Nnaemeka describes women building businesses with seed money, so abolishing money and wages does not fit their economic practice.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: No relevant position in the sources.

one-party-rule.rationale: The Protocol's demand for women's participation in political and decision-making processes presupposes open politics, which makes one-party rule contrary to the programme.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Sources note female chiefs lost power under colonial indirect rule, but give no view on monarchy as an institution.

workers-councils.rationale: No African feminist source proposes councils as the basis of power; the sources discuss women's organising, not this model.

natural-rulers.rationale: The Protocol's non-discrimination and equal participation principles deny that any group is naturally fit to rule, including men over women.

war-builds-character.rationale: Feminist concern with women as victims of armed conflict and the Protocol's peace provisions make glorifying war foreign to the position.

separate-church-state.rationale: Islamic feminism works within religious frameworks while other strands are secular, so adherents are split.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Class is one axis of oppression in stiwanism alongside gender and race, not described as the main driver of history.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Equality is the goal, but the sources do not specify equal outcomes versus opportunity.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Not directly addressed; women's land access is the focus.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Communalism and Motherism's nurture ethic stress community over individual self-interest.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Feminists rely on rights instruments like the Maputo Protocol, so ranking communal duties above individual rights would undercut their programme, although communal values matter to them.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: The sources never judge industrial civilization as a whole; their concern is colonial structures and women's livelihoods.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: Digital privacy and encryption do not appear in the sources.

restore-past-order.rationale: Sources say pre-colonial gender roles were often complementary, but feminists want to modify culture rather than restore the past; Motherism is the nearest case.

direct-action.rationale: Feminists use campaigns and negotiation (#WeAre52, nego-feminism) as well as protest; the sources do not rank direct action against elections.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Sources note gender roles as complementary pre-colonially while seeking change in unequal burdens; no stated abolition.

distribute-by-need.rationale: The sources do not set out a principle of distribution by need versus work.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: The sources critique neo-colonial structures but do not claim that capitalism inevitably produces great-power war.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Nnaemeka and Akob contrast Western individualism with communal values, so rights are not held to belong only to individuals, though the Protocol uses individual rights.

positive-liberty.rationale: The Protocol's economic and social welfare rights reflect the view that rights need material means to be usable.

media-academia-power.rationale: Nnaemeka criticises Western academic theory-making power over African women but does not claim universities and media outrank elected officials.

hereditarian-race.rationale: African feminism opposes colonial and racial hierarchies and the sources give no support for racial genetic hierarchies.

national-rebirth.rationale: The sources do not frame any nation as decadent or in need of rebirth.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Nnaemeka argues that theory formation is imperial and that African women are shut out as knowledge producers, which supports the claim that knowledge reflects power.

universal-morality.rationale: Feminists rely on universal human rights in the Maputo Protocol while resisting Western universalism, as Nnaemeka does in her critique of Okin and Nussbaum.

revive-national-language.rationale: Language revival policy does not appear in the sources.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Motherism, religion-inclusive feminisms and cultural grounding mean reason is not held the only guide.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: The Protocol requires equality before the law, so law enforcing distinct roles is rejected, even though Motherism values complementarity socially.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: African feminism opposes colonial racial and gender hierarchies, and the sources give no support for racial segregation.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Stiwanism critiques colonial and neo-colonial structures but does not state a class theory of the state.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Wikipedia reports that stiwanism and Thiam's multiple jeopardy locate women's oppression in structures, and Ogundipe-Leslie criticised patriarchal systems and internalised patriarchy.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Opposition to racial hierarchy and the rejection of colonial categories leave no basis for discouraging mixed marriage.

night-watchman-state.rationale: The Protocol assigns the state many duties for women's welfare, education and health, which contradicts a night-watchman state.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The Maputo Protocol is built on non-discrimination, dignity and equal rights for women, which states equal worth and equal protection before the law.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: The Protocol seeks equal marital and inheritance rights regardless of custom, but Muslim and customary-law objections show adherents divide on overriding personal law.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Cattle slaughter law is not an African feminist concern in the sources.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Women's right to take part in political and decision-making processes in Article 9 rests on the idea that authority needs the participation of the governed.

population-transfer.rationale: Forcing out a minority conflicts with the Protocol's dignity and non-discrimination provisions and with peace commitments.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Nego-feminism's no-ego collaboration stresses cooperation over struggle as the engine of progress.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Stiwanism treats rural and poor women's conditions as the core concern of social transformation.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Stiwanism explains women's poverty by colonial and neo-colonial structures, not by population.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: The sources hold that Africa's diversity is a given and rule out a single feminism, without treating diversity as a threat.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Ogundipe-Leslie centred rural women's hardships, not any claim that rural life is healthier.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Nnaemeka's own critique targets Western theory, not educated people in general, and the tradition is largely academic and literary.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Nnaemeka rejects the idea that Western feminism and moral universals can judge African practices, supporting a view of cultures as different rather than ranked.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: The Protocol's education and reproductive-health provisions support sexual and gender education for girls and boys, though sexuality remains contested.

religious-exemptions.rationale: The Protocol sets limits on harmful customary practice, while religious freedom is also valued, so adherents are split.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Stiwanism holds that colonial and neo-colonial structures must be transformed along with the position of women.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Peace emphasis points against nuclear arms.

sacred-ruler.rationale: A sacred hereditary ruler contradicts equal rights and participation; and sources note colonial and customary male rulers curtailed women.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Equal protection and accountability under the Protocol leave no room for rulers above the law.

land-redistribution.rationale: Sources document that men controlled land and income under colonialism and that women farm most food, which supports giving land to those who work it.

women-must-cover.rationale: Feminists oppose compulsion over women's bodies, and even Islamic feminism works for equality, not mandatory covering by law.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Stiwanism treats economic structure as one of several factors, not the main driver.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: The Protocol protects women's rights against customary majorities, implying courts should constrain them.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: The article records Kenya's #WeAre52 campaign for a two-thirds gender cap in governing bodies, and Article 9 of the Protocol requires women's participation in decision-making.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Nnaemeka's call for African women as knowledge producers on African terms supports teaching history from African centres.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Ogundipe-Leslie ascribed women's plight partly to imposed colonial structures and rejected defining African feminism through Euro-America.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: The Protocol's non-discrimination principle and anti-discrimination aims reject private discrimination.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: The Protocol itself is a binding rights instrument that constrains government; Wikipedia reports 44 ratifications.

elective-rulers.rationale: Article 9 on participation in political processes and campaigns for women's seats assume elected leadership.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: The tradition is built on women's participation in politics and decision-making, the opposite of withdrawal.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Nnaemeka favours local priorities in development but no rejection of aid is stated.

male-disadvantage-attention.rationale: The sources say African feminists see men as facing hardships of their own and favour including them, though the programme centres women.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Nnaemeka rejects Western theory formation as imperial and holds African women do feminism on their own terms, which supports locally shaped institutions.

filial-duty.rationale: Communalism and family values are central to African feminist writers such as Aidoo and Acholonu.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Customary land tenure disadvantaged women according to the sources, so adherents have no single view on communal land holding.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: African feminists work with international donors while criticising Western agendas; no stated support for restrictions.

non-intervention.rationale: Nnaemeka rejects outside rescue interventions yet the Protocol is a regional rights norm, so adherents mix.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Conspiracy claims against a minority conflict with non-discrimination and dignity.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: The Protocol regulates marriage in women's interest, so abolishing legal marriage is not its approach, and family is valued by many adherents.

informal-organisation.rationale: Nnaemeka describes informal women's networks and savings groups, but the sources do not oppose permanent organisations.

national-law-over-international.rationale: African feminists rely on international and continental treaties like the Maputo Protocol, so primacy of national law is disfavoured.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: The Protocol assigns duties to states but not on provider mix.

religion-illusion.rationale: The sources treat Islam and Christianity as fields that African feminists reinterpret from within rather than illusions to outgrow, which supports disagreement; secular strands such as Thiam's make a strong rejection unrepresentative.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: Stiwanism links women's liberation to wider social transformation including class and neo-colonial structures.

socialized-care.rationale: Sources value motherhood and family while seeking recognition of women's burdens, so adherents are split.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Nnaemeka describes cooperative savings groups but not a society reorganised in cooperative communities.

holocaust-denial.rationale: No support in the sources; the commitment to dignity and anti-racism excludes denial.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Nyanzi notes most African feminists resist challenging heterosexism, but queer African feminists and rights framing oppose criminalisation, leaving adherents divided with a lean against.

suppress-opposition.rationale: The programme's insistence on participation and rights rules out suppressing opposition.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: The article says colonialism weakened women's status and removed female chiefs' power, so adherents oppose colonial rule for the metropole's benefit.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Article 9's right to participation and women's local organising support wide participation in decisions.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: Awa Thiam's multiple jeopardy holds that sex, class and colonial or racial oppression combine, and Wikipedia notes intersectionality is welcomed but judged insufficient.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: Some queer African feminists back it, but the majority resist challenging heterosexism, so adherents are split.

islam-incompatible.rationale: The article describes Islamic feminism in Africa working inside Islam for gender equality, so adherents reject claims of incompatibility with modern values.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Muslim, Christian and secular strands differ.

rich-first.rationale: Stiwanism's concern with inclusive transformation leans against letting some grow rich first.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Equal participation conflicts with hereditary succession.

domination-women-nature.rationale: Motherism links motherhood, nature and nurture, and its aim of complementarity between humans and nature supports shared liberation.

racial-franchise.rationale: The sources hold no support for racial limits on voting; the tradition opposes colonial racial hierarchy.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Targeting a minority conflicts with non-discrimination and dignity.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: The article describes Islamic revivalist feminists and others seeking gender equality within an Islamic framework, which is reinterpretation of religion.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: Most African feminists resist challenging heterosexism, a minority back LGBT rights, so adherents are split.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Religion is a field of feminist engagement in Africa and not treated as something for the state to remove.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: The Protocol assigns welfare duties to states, so charity alone is not favoured.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: Nana Asma'u's women's education movement and Islamic feminists seeking equality indicate support for women's religious roles; leadership offices are not specified.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: The Maputo Protocol sets equal rights and shared responsibility between spouses in marriage as a core provision on marriage and divorce.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: No stated position; most adherents would not demand strict pacifism.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Sources show gender roles changing under colonialism, so continuity from ancient origins is not their view.

no-fixed-category-of-women.rationale: The article says Africa's diversity rules out a single feminist theory, and stiwanism treats class, religion and marital status as shaping women's experiences.

scripture-judged-by-women.rationale: Islamic feminists seek equality within religion, but adherents of other strands do not use scripture as the test, so they split.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Africana womanism emphasises Black women's own politics but others reject race organising, so adherents split.

racial-pride.rationale: Africana womanism, rooted in Black life, and the break from white feminism endorse pride in African ancestry.

women-distinct-values.rationale: Motherism places motherhood and nurture at the core, and nego-feminism draws on maternal ideas, though not all strands claim distinct values.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: Ogundipe-Leslie's critique of neo-colonial structures supports reshaping international economic rules.

shared-human-nature.rationale: Nnaemeka resists Western universals, while the Protocol assumes shared rights, so adherents split.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: Peace emphasis leans against nuclear arsenals.

property-franchise.rationale: Limiting the vote by wealth contradicts equal participation rights and the sources' record of women excluded from land and income.

ban-fgm.rationale: The Maputo Protocol seeks an end to female genital mutilation and Wikipedia lists FGM among the major problems facing African women.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: The Protocol includes rights to inheritance and widows' rights, and the sources document men's control of land under colonial and customary rule.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: Criminal sentencing policy is outside what the sources address.

premarital-sex.rationale: Wikipedia notes that sexuality is the issue on which strands differ most: some reject Western sexual liberation, others defend women's sexual autonomy.

women-suffrage.rationale: The Maputo Protocol commits states to women's equal participation in political life, and equal political rights are a basic aim of the movement.

religion-oppresses-women.rationale: Wikipedia describes African feminists as divided: some criticise religion's role in patriarchy while others stress its place in African life and see religion as often supporting women.

gendered-self-government.rationale: The Maputo Protocol commits states to women's participation in political and decision-making processes, and African feminism seeks equality from the outset of post-colonial arrangements.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: The Maputo Protocol's rights to life, dignity and security of person are incompatible with killing suspects without trial.

material-over-identity.rationale: African feminists hold that sex, class and race oppressions combine, so they reject concentrating on material interests alone.

missingStatements.text: Female genital mutilation should be prohibited by law.
missingStatements.rationale: The Maputo Protocol seeks an end to female genital mutilation and Wikipedia lists FGM among the major problems facing African women.

missingStatements.text: Women should have the same legal right as men to inherit and own land.
missingStatements.rationale: The Protocol includes rights to inheritance and widows' rights, and the sources document men's control of land under colonial and customary rule.

missingStatements.text: Women's rights are best advanced by negotiating with men and community institutions rather than by confronting them.
missingStatements.rationale: Nnaemeka's nego-feminism and snail-sense feminism stress negotiation and working with men, though stiwanism also demands wider transformation.
missingStatements.declined: A question of method rather than position, and contested within African feminism itself.

notes: Strands diverge: nego-feminism and Motherism stress negotiation, complementarity and family; stiwanism and Thiam stress structural and class transformation; a minority of queer African feminists challenge heterosexism that most others leave unquestioned. Sources opened were partly secondary (Wikipedia); only Nnaemeka's essay is a primary text, and the Maputo Protocol's article wording was not read directly.
